context: Marie Tharp arrived at Columbia University in 1948 «with two master’s degrees, and almost no prospect» of going to sea.

choices.text: with two master’s degrees and almost no prospect
with two master’s degrees; and almost no prospect
with two master’s degrees and, almost no prospect

why.A: "almost no prospect of going to sea" is not an independent clause, so comma + FANBOYS is illegal here.
why.B: Correct — two compound objects of the same preposition need no comma.
why.C: A semicolon requires a complete sentence on both sides.
why.D: A comma cannot separate a conjunction from what follows it.

context: Research vessels of the era «do not accept» women aboard, so Tharp worked from a drafting table.

why.A: Present tense clashes with the past-tense "worked" later in the same sentence.
why.B: Future tense is impossible for a historical fact.
why.C: Correct — matches the established past tense of the surrounding narrative.
why.D: Present progressive contradicts the historical setting.

context: For four years she plotted depth readings, «one single line at a time, one after another.»

choices.text: one single line at a time.
one line at a time, in sequence, individually.

why.A: "one single" is redundant and "one after another" repeats "at a time."
why.B: "one single" still says the same thing twice.
why.C: Correct — the shortest phrasing that keeps the full meaning.
why.D: Piles up three synonymous modifiers.

context: «Plotting depth readings for four years, the drafting paper revealed» a mountain range running down the center of the Atlantic.

choices.text: Plotting depth readings for four years, Tharp saw emerge on her drafting paper
Plotted for four years, the depth readings on drafting paper revealed
After four years of plotting depth readings, the paper showed

why.A: Dangling modifier — drafting paper cannot plot readings.
why.B: Correct — places Tharp, the actual plotter, immediately after the modifier.
why.C: Readings do not plot themselves either; the actor is still missing.
why.D: "the paper" still did not do the four years of plotting.

context: Splitting that range lengthwise was a deep V-shaped notch «— a rift valley.»

why.A: Correct — a single dash after a complete clause may introduce an appositive for emphasis.
why.B: Also defensible in isolation, but ACT will not offer two fully correct choices; the dash is what the sentence’s emphatic reveal calls for.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it.
why.D: A closing dash at the end of a sentence is not a real construction.

context: Tharp recognized what the valley implied. If the seafloor was pulling apart along that seam, then continents were moving, «a idea» then associated with Alfred Wegener.

why.A: "a" cannot precede a vowel sound.
why.B: Correct — "an" before the vowel sound in "idea."
why.C: "and" creates a nonsensical list.
why.D: "ideal" changes the meaning entirely.

context: Heezen dismissed her interpretation as "girl talk" and asked her to redraw the maps. «Therefore,» she redrew them. The rift valley appeared again.

why.A: "Therefore" implies the redrawing follows logically as a conclusion, which flattens the passage’s point.
why.B: "Nevertheless" wrongly signals that she redrew them despite being asked to.
why.C: The redrawing is not an example of anything.

context: It appeared in the North Atlantic, «in profiles from the Indian Ocean, and the Pacific was another place it appeared.»

the Indian Ocean profiles, and appearing in the Pacific.
in the Indian Ocean, also the Pacific.

why.A: The third item switches to a full clause, breaking parallel structure.
why.B: Correct — three parallel prepositional phrases beginning with "in."
why.C: Mixes a noun phrase with a participial phrase.
why.D: "also the Pacific" is not parallel and creates a comma splice feel.

context: When Heezen overlaid the locations of recorded undersea earthquakes onto Tharp’s maps, the pattern of epicenters «trace» the rift valley almost exactly.

why.A: The subject is "pattern," singular, and the passage is in past tense.
why.B: Still plural, and the added pronoun is redundant.
why.C: Correct — singular subject "pattern" plus past tense to match the narrative.
why.D: Present perfect breaks the established past-tense sequence.

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence "Heezen dismissed her interpretation as ‘girl talk.’" If deleted, the paragraph would primarily lose:

evidence that Heezen was not a competent scientist.
a transition to the paragraph about plate tectonics.
nothing of significance, since the resistance is stated elsewhere.

context: The maps «Tharp’s and Heezen’s» published in 1957 changed how the public pictured the planet.

why.B: Correct — a compound subject with no possession requires no apostrophe.
why.C: Adds incorrect plurals to proper names.
why.D: Introduces a possessive where none belongs.

context: Plate tectonics, the framework that now organizes all of geology, «rests substantially on» the seafloor she drew.

why.A: Correct — matches the passage’s measured, formal register.

context: They are met by a dozen volunteers with soldering irons, sewing machines, and «a rule; nobody repairs anything for you.»

a rule, nobody repairs anything for you.
a rule nobody repairs anything for you.

context: «I starting coming two years ago» with a toaster that had stopped toasting.

Starting to come two years ago

context: Ellis, «a retired elevator mechanic handed» me a screwdriver and waited.

context: Inside was not the mysterious machinery I expected, «it was a spring, a lever, and a corroded strip of metal.»

it being a spring, a lever, and a corroded strip of metal.

why.B: Present tense contradicts the completed span.

was prepared and ready to discard one
had been ready to throw one away in the trash

why.B: Correct — removes both redundancies without losing meaning.

context: The economics were not the point; the habit was. «In addition,» the Repair Café movement began in Amsterdam in 2009 and has since spread to more than two thousand locations.

why.A: "In addition" implies the new paragraph adds to the previous point, but it shifts to background information.
why.B: The movement’s founding is not a consequence of the writer’s realization.

context: Its organizers keep careful records: what came in, what was fixed, what could not be. «Roughly two-thirds of items leaves» working.

that the volunteers insist it is also a kind of success.
and the volunteers insist is also a kind of success.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence "He never once took the screwdriver out of my hand." Where would it most logically be placed?

stem: Which choice best concludes the essay by tying back to its opening image of broken things?

why.A: Present tense clashes with the completed historical span.
